title: What Are the Different Types of HVAC Systems?
h1: What Are the Main Types of HVAC Systems for Homes?
description: From split systems and heat pumps to mini-splits and packaged units, here are the main types of home HVAC systems and where each one makes sense.
quick_answer: The main types of home HVAC systems are split systems (a furnace or air handler inside with an AC outside), heat pump systems, ductless mini-splits, packaged units, and dual fuel hybrids. Older homes may also have wall or floor furnaces. Most San Diego and Orange County homes use a ducted split system with the furnace in the attic, garage or a closet.
body:
What is a split system?

A split system is the most common setup in local homes. It has an indoor unit, usually a gas furnace, and an outdoor air conditioner connected by refrigerant lines. The furnace blower moves air across an AC coil on top of it and sends heated or cooled air through ducts.

Good fit for: homes with existing ductwork and a gas line. Swapping one out for a newer split system is usually the most straightforward replacement.

How is a heat pump system different?

A heat pump looks a lot like a split AC, but it can run in reverse to heat the home. Instead of a gas furnace, the indoor unit is an electric air handler, often with backup heat strips. One outdoor unit handles both heating and cooling.

Good fit for: our mild climate, homes going all-electric, and homes without gas service. Coastal and most inland winters are well within what modern heat pumps handle.

What are ductless mini-splits?

Mini-splits use an outdoor unit connected by small refrigerant lines to one or more indoor heads mounted on walls or ceilings. There are no ducts. Each head has its own temperature setting, and most mini-splits are heat pumps, so they heat and cool.

Good fit for: room additions, converted garages, ADUs, older homes with no ducts, and rooms that never get comfortable on the main system.

What other types of systems are out there?

  • Packaged units: everything is in one cabinet, usually on the roof or beside the house, with ducts running inside. Common in commercial buildings and some homes without attic or closet space for equipment.
  • Dual fuel (hybrid) systems: a heat pump paired with a gas furnace. The heat pump handles most heating, and the furnace takes over when it's the better option.
  • Wall and floor furnaces: gas heaters built into a wall or floor without ducts. Common in older homes and many smaller houses built decades ago. They heat but don't cool.
  • Evaporative coolers: sometimes called swamp coolers. They cool by adding moisture to the air, so they work better in dry inland heat than in humid coastal air.
  • Radiant heat: hot water tubing or electric elements in floors or ceilings. Comfortable and quiet, but it doesn't cool and is less common here.
  • Geothermal heat pumps: use buried loops to exchange heat with the ground. Very efficient, but installation is involved and they're rare in local homes.

How can you tell what kind of system you have?

Look at the indoor unit. A gas furnace has a flue pipe running up through the roof and a gas line. An electric air handler has neither. If the outdoor unit's label says heat pump, or your thermostat has an emergency heat setting, you likely have a heat pump. No ducts and wall-mounted heads means a mini-split. A single big cabinet outside with ducts running into the house is a packaged unit.

How do you choose the right type for your home?

The best system depends on what the house already has and how you live in it. A technician will look at:

  • Whether you have ductwork, and what condition it's in
  • Whether you have gas service and what your electrical panel can support
  • Where equipment can go, such as the attic, garage, a hall closet or the side yard
  • Whether some rooms run hotter or colder than others
  • How close you are to the coast, since salt air affects outdoor units
  • Your plans for the home, like an addition or going all-electric

Sizing matters as much as type. A load calculation that looks at your insulation, windows, orientation and square footage keeps you from ending up with a system that's too big or too small.

What about zoning?

Zoning isn't a separate system type. It's an add-on that uses dampers in the ducts and multiple thermostats so one system can send air to different areas as needed. It's useful in two-story homes where upstairs runs hot.

If you're not sure what you have or what to replace it with, our HVAC team can look at your home and lay out the options with a free estimate.
faqs: What is the most common HVAC system in Southern California homes?
A ducted split system with a gas furnace inside and an air conditioner outside. The furnace is usually in the attic, garage or a hall closet in local homes.
Is a heat pump better than a furnace and AC?
It depends on the home. Heat pumps work well in our mild climate and run on electricity only. A furnace and AC may make sense if you have gas and want strong heat on cold inland nights.
Can I add air conditioning to a home with a wall furnace?
Yes. Common options are a ductless mini-split or a new ducted system if there's space for ductwork. A technician can look at the layout and electrical panel to see what fits.
Do swamp coolers work near the coast?
Not as well. Evaporative coolers rely on dry air to cool, so they're more effective in hot, dry inland areas than in humid coastal neighborhoods.
